question: What is the main goal of injection safety in your daily clinical practice?

options.A: Administering medication without causing harm to patients or yourself
options.B: Using only intravenous routes for fluid replacement
options.C: Ensuring every patient gets at least one daily injection
options.D: Disposing of all used syringes in household trash bins

explanation: You've got this! Injection safety is all about protecting everyone—patients, healthcare workers, and the community—from any harm related to injections. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h1)

question: Why are nurses so important when it comes to keeping injection safety protocols working?

options.A: Nurses are the only staff legally allowed to handle medical waste
options.B: Nurses write the hospital policies regarding medication purchases
options.C: Nurses manufacture all disposable syringes used in hospitals
options.D: Nurses administer the majority of clinical injections daily

explanation: Spot on! Since you and your fellow nurses give most of the injections, your daily habits directly keep safety standards alive on the ward. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h1)

question: Which viral infection is most commonly linked globally to unsafe injections?
explanation: Well done! Along with Hepatitis C and HIV, Hepatitis B is one of the main bloodborne pathogens spread when injection safety rules are broken. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h2)

question: What is the main reason developing countries experience more complications from unsafe injections?

options.A: A complete lack of trained nurses in regional clinics
options.B: Patients refusing oral medications in favor of injections
options.C: The natural resistance of tropical germs to standard soap
options.D: Supply shortages and poor waste management systems

explanation: Exactly. When clinics struggle with equipment shortages, it can unfortunately lead to dangerous workarounds like reusing syringes. You're building great clinical awareness! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h2)

question: What is the dangerous practice of using the same syringe barrel for more than one patient called?
explanation: You nailed it! Reusing syringes—even if you change the needle—transfers microscopic amounts of blood and fluids between patients, spreading serious infections. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h3)

question: In a busy clinic, how does a multi-dose medication vial usually get contaminated?

options.A: Using a previously used needle or syringe to enter the vial
options.B: Cleaning the rubber stopper with alcohol before every puncture
options.C: Storing the medicine bottle inside a warm medication refrigerator
options.D: Failing to shake the suspension liquid before drawing a dose

explanation: That's right! If a needle has touched a patient, using it to enter a shared multi-dose vial contaminates the whole bottle for everyone else. Always use a fresh, sterile needle and syringe! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h3)

question: Which bloodborne virus is known to survive on environmental surfaces for several days?
explanation: Good job! Hepatitis B is remarkably hardy and can stay infectious on surfaces outside the body for quite a while, which is why strict disinfection matters so much. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h4)

question: What creates the direct pathway for spreading disease during an unsafe injection?

options.A: Inhaling medication droplets while prepping a syringe
options.B: A contaminated needle breaking the skin and entering circulation
options.C: Swallowing oral tablets without enough water
options.D: Touching a sealed medication package with bare hands

explanation: Spot on! Injections bypass your skin's natural defense barrier, meaning any germs on a dirty needle go straight into the patient's tissues and bloodstream. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h4)

question: What is a major community-wide effect when a clinic suffers an outbreak of healthcare-associated infections?

options.A: Loss of public trust in the healthcare system
options.B: Lower costs for public health insurance programs
options.C: An immediate surplus of available hospital beds
options.D: Increased willingness of patients to receive injections

explanation: Exactly. When a clinic spreads disease instead of healing, people lose faith and may stop seeking care when they truly need it. Safe nursing builds community trust! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h5)

question: If a patient catches Hepatitis C from a poorly sterilized procedure, what long-term organ damage are they most at risk for?

options.D: Permanent paralysis of the lower limbs

explanation: You got it! Hepatitis C attacks the liver, often causing long-term inflammation and scarring over time. Protecting patients from bloodborne infections is a huge part of our job. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h5)

question: What is one of the most common workplace hazards for nurses during medication rounds?
explanation: Spot on! Needle-stick injuries are a constant hazard on the ward, which is why practicing safe handling techniques every single day is so crucial for your own safety. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h6)

question: Besides the risk of physical infection, what immediate emotional impact does a needle-stick injury often have on a nurse?

options.A: Complete temporary paralysis of the affected hand
options.B: Immediate dismissal from their nursing position
options.C: Automatic immunity to all future bloodborne viruses
options.D: Severe psychological stress and anxiety while waiting for test results

explanation: So true. Waiting for screening results after a needle poke can cause a lot of worry and sleepless nights. That's why prevention is always your best friend! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h6)

question: If you absolutely must recap a used needle, what is the safest technique to use?

options.B: Holding the cap tightly in the palm of your hand
options.C: Pushing the needle directly into the cap using both hands
options.D: Asking a colleague to hold the cap while you insert the needle

explanation: Brilliant! The one-handed scoop method keeps your free hand safely away from the sharp tip so you don't accidentally poke yourself. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h7)

question: Why are single-dose medication vials much better for infection control than multi-dose vials?

options.A: They completely eliminate the risk of cross-contamination between patients
options.B: They contain larger volumes of liquid for multiple shifts
options.C: They are always cheaper for hospital procurement to buy
options.D: They never require alcohol swabbing of the rubber top

explanation: You got it! Since single-dose vials are used for just one patient, there's zero chance of a contaminated needle transferring germs to the next dose. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h7)

question: Where is the best place to set up a sharps disposal container in a patient care area?

options.A: On the floor underneath the nurse's station desk
options.B: Inside the central facility storage warehouse
options.C: Inside the clean utility supply cupboard
options.D: As close as possible to where the injection is given

explanation: Spot on! Keeping sharps bins right at the point of use means you never have to walk across the room carrying an exposed needle. Safety first! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h8)

question: What major hazard happens when sharps disposal boxes are allowed to become overfilled?

options.A: Rapid evaporation of liquid medications stored inside
options.B: Chemical reactions that dissolve the plastic bin
options.C: Foul odors spreading throughout the hospital ward
options.D: Higher risk of accidental needle pricks for staff and waste handlers

explanation: Exactly! When bins are stuffed too full, needles start poking out and endangering everyone nearby. Always swap out sharps bins before they hit the fill line! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h8)

question: How can you, as a bedside nurse, help improve injection safety standards in your clinic?

options.A: By buying new safety syringes with your own personal money
options.B: By reporting unsafe practices and joining safety audits
options.C: By handling all medical waste disposal completely alone
options.D: By refusing to give any injections during night shifts

explanation: Well done! Speaking up about risks and taking part in safety checks helps fix system flaws and protects everyone. You're thinking like a professional nurse! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h9)

question: You notice your clinic frequently runs out of single-use syringes, causing staff to reuse equipment. What is your best professional action?

options.A: Keep quiet so you don't upset the clinic manager during a busy shift
options.B: Buy plastic syringes from a local pharmacy using your own money
options.C: Stop giving all prescribed medications until the hospital closes
options.D: Report the shortage through official channels and advocate for safer supplies

explanation: Spot on! As a nurse, you have a duty to advocate for your patients and push for proper resources when safety is on the line. Great clinical leadership! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h9)
